utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I assume this is Mr. Jozo Vrebac? Good morning. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vrebac. Tell me, please, can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The witness is a little hard of hearing, so if you can't hear us, please let us know. The witness says he would like the volume to be switched on. Could the usher help the witness with the volume, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it better now? Is it all right? Yes? Let us begin, Mr. Vrebac. Will you please introduce yourself, tell the Court your full name, where you were born, your occupation, and where you reside. You don't have to get up; remain seated.

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: My name is Jozo Vrebac. I was born on the 30th of September, 1927, in Santici, Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your occupation?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I'm a metal worker, now retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, tell me, were you living in Santici on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a shelter in your house, or in your daughter's house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: There is a basement which serves as a shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is in your daughter's house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, is it a real shelter, what kind of a basement it is, and how it came to be used as a shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: This basement was built as a basement for the house. When the JNA started shelling, it served as a shelter from the air raids.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell me, was there any kind of special equipment in that basement, as is normal in shelters, like beds, blankets, first-aid kits, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we saw some photographs of that house and that shelter, so we won't tire Their Honours with those photographs again. But tell us, please, how many rooms it had, and what is the area?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: There are three premises, three rooms, and the total area is nine and a half metres by eight metres, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now focus on the 16th of April, 1993, and could you tell the Court where you were on that day, whether you went to the shelter, and tell us about how you spent that whole day. Not too quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I was awakened in the morning by villagers who were coming to the shelter. I went to the shelter, came back to the house, and woke up my son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you came back to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, I kept visiting both houses, my own and my daughter's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, your house and your daughter's house, what is the distance between them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: About 13 or 14 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they are very close to one another?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend that whole day in the shelter, in the vicinity and nearby?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, all day and all night I was thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly were you doing? Were you sitting in one particular room? Tell us a little more about what you did.

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I was trying to help people and provide them with whatever they needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you acted the host?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vrebac, do you know Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic and his family well?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long have you known them, and how well?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Ever since his childhood, and throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That morning, on the 16th of April, did you see any member of Vlatko Kupreskic's family in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I saw Vlatko, his mother, his wife, and his two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us at what time you saw Vlatko for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: At about 6.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us what Vlatko looked like?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: He looked terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why terrible?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: He was terrified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to him at all?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Just then, it was not possible to talk to him, he was in such bad shape, and as he is a heart patient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you well, he was afraid?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was very frightened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed? Was he dressed in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you surprised to see Vlatko in the shelter for people unfit for military service?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Because I know that he has a bad heart, that he never served in the army, nor was he a member of any unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me now how much time Vlatko spent there in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: He was there roughly until about 10.00, roughly. I couldn't tell you exactly until when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him leave?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And he said he was going to see whether his father was alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where his father was?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: His father had stayed behind in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: He told me when he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Vlatko again on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I did, at 16.00 hours, something like that, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see him, when he returned?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, just when he came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to him then?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: He said that his father was alive but he couldn't transport him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: He has a broken leg, and he had kind of braces on his legs and he couldn't move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any shooting?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was coming back. Was that perhaps one of the reasons why he couldn't come back?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: No, not really, but his father couldn't walk and there was a bit of shooting too, so that he didn't dare risk it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Vlatko go back again to fetch his father?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, in the evening at dusk, he went to fetch his father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he manage to bring him over?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He brought him to the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Well, it was night-time, I know. I didn't look at my watch, what time it was when he came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see Vlatko's father as well when he came?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, I personally saw both his father and him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, when did Vlatko and his family leave the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: His family and all the people who were in the basement left that shelter on the second day in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the next day, the 17th, in the evening. Do you know where they went?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: They went in the direction of Radakov Most to Rovna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question for you. Could you please tell us, regarding the people whose names I'm going to list, whether you saw them in the shelter on the 16th of April, 1993? Did you see Ivo Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Ruza Grgic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Ljubo Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Alojz Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Gordana Cuic Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, with her mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Ankica Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vrebac. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Counsel Par. Yes, cross-examination by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vrebac, just a few questions. Do you know the parents of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are their names?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: His father's name is Anto, and their mother's name is Luca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you on good terms with them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Of course I was. How could I say otherwise?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them on that day, the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I saw them in the shelter, in the shelter on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was with them from the Kupreskic family?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Mirjan's mother-in-law, his wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mirjan's wife?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, his two children and mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remember anything in connection with the mother-in-law? Did you see how she was feeling?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: She sat in the shelter in the way she would sit at home, but Mirjan brought her in a wheelbarrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she have any problems moving?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I don't know. Yes. She couldn't move on her own. She was disabled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, do you know whether they too left for Rovna the next day?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Everyone left for Rovna, all the people who were in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Mr. Rebac, good morning to you. My name is Michael Blaxill, and I'm one of the prosecuting counsel in this case, and I do have some questions I would like to ask you as a result of what you have told the Chamber. Cross-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you were awakened by some fellow villagers on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993. Do you remember what time that was, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: It was about 5.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall the names of the villagers who woke you up?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: There was a large group, so I can't tell you each individual's name. But I know them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give an estimate then of the number in that group? You say it is large. How many people do you think it was; 10, 20, 30?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Roughly, about 25 to 30 families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just give an indication as to what was the general mood of those people? Did they appear to you to be anxious or frightened, or what were they like?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: They were all frightened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they arrived at your house, sir. Did you then guide them across to your daughter's house 13 metres away?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I ran over, unlocked the door and came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did those people just go into the building and into the basement, and you returned to your own home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, had you had much of an opportunity to get dressed in outdoor clothing?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: When I came back home, then I got dressed properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of clothing did you wear when you got dressed properly?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: The usual clothes I wear at home every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe, for instance, whether you were wearing a jacket of some description, and if so, what colour it was?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I never wore a jacket. I wore a suit of this kind, but it was an older one, and normal shoes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask again, sir, do you recall the colour of that clothing you put on?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I usually wear brown or black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you now be precise and remember which it was that you wore that day?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I really don't know, because I too was excited and frightened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time at around 5.00, was there any kind of shooting going on in the vicinity, or could you hear any?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: About 5.00, there wasn't any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then made aware by the people, or were you aware for some other reason, as to why everybody was frightened?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I have no idea. They didn't tell me. I just know that if there is any kind of an alarm, people went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So are you suggesting, sir, that you were agitated because clearly these people all turned up at the shelter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You returned to your home. Do you recall how long you remained in your home before you paid your next visit to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I went back home just to wake up my son who was upstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then perhaps we can say within a very few minutes, you then returned to the shelter. Would this be something like quarter past 5.00 in the morning, something of that order?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back, you say there was 25 to 30 families. How many people in all do you think that was? Was that 50, 60 people or more?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: On the average, you can count that there were three people to a family, on the average.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we take a rough average of, say, 75 to 80 people you say then went into the basement rooms in your daughter's home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So with a measurement you've given of, I think, nine and a half by eight metres, would it be fair to say that it was very crowded down there in those three basement rooms?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: It was, of course, crowded like a matchbox.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing the arrival of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic and any members of his family?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall at about what time they arrived at the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: They arrived at about 6.00, when the shooting was on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying, sir, that the shooting had started somewhere around 20 past 5.00 that morning, something like that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Perhaps you are right. I can't know exactly whether it was 5.20 or half past 5.00. I wasn't looking at the watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. So there was now shooting going on outside. The Kupreskic family arrived. Do you recall into which room they went?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say which one that was?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: The children and his wife went downstairs, and Vlatko stayed sitting on a bench in the hallway to rest a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that time, sir, would it be true to say you also were in the hallway of your daughter's house; is that where you were located at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I was all over the place, wherever it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Saying that you were all over the place, you've already indicated that you tried to provide some sort of provisions and assistance to the people sheltering. Did that entail you going backwards and forwards to your own home quite frequently?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For instance, could you tell me, the first time that you went home to your house after you encountered Vlatko Kupreskic, what time was that that you went back to your house for the next occasion; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: They went up there, and while they were in there, I went back to the house and I said to my wife to boil the milk -- she had already milked the cow -- so that she should take it to the house and give it to the children there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall at what time you had that conversation with your wife?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: It is hard for one to tell each and every minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, for instance, how many visits you made back to your own house up to the time when Vlatko, you say, left the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I spent more time in that house than in my own, with the people there, because we also used the ground floor and the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again I would ask you, do you remember, though, how many times you actually did have to go back to your own home up to the point where Vlatko left the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during this period we still have shooting going on in the area that is clearly audible to you all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: We could hear the shooting all over, but later on it subsided, around 9.00 or something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you had no reason necessarily to look at your watch and see what time it was when -- what time it was when the shooting subsided?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: It never even occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you were far too preoccupied with the danger and with trying to help the people, really, to pay attention to the time? Would that be fair, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew the majority of the people in that shelter quite well, I would imagine, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I knew them all, each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall, for instance, the name of the family or a particular person who arrived immediately after Vlatko Kupreskic's family? Does that strike a chord in your memory?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you say you recall the arrival of the family of Vlatko Kupreskic. Can you recall the names of the family that arrived immediately after them, if there was one?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I recall also Anto Vidovic, who also brought his wife, in a wheelbarrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when certain names were put to you by Mr. Par, like Ivo Vidovic, Ruza Grgic, Ljuba Vidovic, do you recall whether any of those people actually left the shelter at all during the early part of that morning?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: That morning, those who entered the shelter could come out only to the door, to the terrace which was in front of the door, to go out on to the terrace and see what was on fire, because houses were aflame, and we did not know which houses. I didn't know either, so I would go out every once in a while to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But clearly at some later point Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic left the shelter, because you say you spoke to him, and he told you he was going to see about his father; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody else, to your recollection, leave the shelter, perhaps to go and look to the safety of family, or to the safety of their animals or something?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during the course of that morning, sir, if we have the picture correctly, you were doing your best to assist a large group of people in a very confined space and all of whom were very frightened for their safety; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I didn't hear you properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of the morning, if we see the picture correctly, you were endeavouring to assist a large group of people who were in a very confined space and in a very frightening situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have confirmed more than once, sir, that, you know, you didn't spend your time looking at the watch and checking what time various things happened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: It is. There were old people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, one further thing I would say. You have today said that you recall Vlatko Kupreskic leaving the shelter at 10.00. Can you now really say that you can be so sure of the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around 10.00. Would be it true to say, though, that you didn't look at your watch at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Well, we halted there, and we talked, and we looked at the time just about then, because it was at the corner of my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall a lady by the name of -- I hope I say it correctly -- Cuic, Mrs. Gordana Cuic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Gordana what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps it's Cujic. My own linguistic limitations; I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness might know her maiden name, and she was Gordana Cuic, married, Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: Gordana Vidovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether that lady left the premises at any time, left the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: No, she didn't. She stayed there with her mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm obliged to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Par --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm also obliged to Counsel Par for assisting me with my linguistic problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Only one question for the witness. Re-examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vrebac, when I asked you if you saw that Ivo Vidovic was in the shelter that day, you said he was. Did Ivo Vidovic spend the whole day in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when did you see him?

utterances.speaker: JOZO VREBAC
utterances.text: I saw him that morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have any questions. I assume there's no objection to the witness being released. Mr. Vrebac, thank you so much for coming to The Hague to give evidence in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, too. All the best to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, on the 7th of May this year, the Trial Chamber adopted a calendar of witness testimonies, and it was concluded that as of the 25th of May until the 4th of June, we would be having witnesses relative to a defence of Vlatko Kupreskic; after that, witnesses testifying in favour of Drago Josipovic would be talking. So today I need to talk to the Witness and Victim Protection Unit, so I need to know if the schedule is still the same, so that Drago Josipovic's witnesses could be asked to come here between the 21st of June and 26th of June. Could the Trial Chamber help me to set the date with the Witness Protection Unit to organise their arrival in The Hague and the time of their appearance before the Court? (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm afraid we don't have our diary close at hand, but after the break, I will let you know when we resume in late June. I think we will stick to the schedule which we had agreed upon previously, but I'll let you know afterwards. Thank you. We could now -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, may I clarify something very briefly. Under D26 (sic), we have prepared a set of documents relative to the testimony of Dragica Krizanac. My attention has been drawn to the fact that when these documents were copied, something was not done properly; that is, not all pages were copied. So I saw to it in the meantime, and I should like to ask you to look at those documents now. These are documents under 00637483 to 00637510. I have a sufficient number of copies for Your Honours and for the registry and for the Prosecution, and I should like to ask the usher to help me distribute them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I am sorry. I've just been told that there's a mistake in the transcript: Not D26, D two six; that is, 2/6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. All right. So these documents will be handed to the Prosecution and the Court, and I wonder whether we could bring in the next witness. So this is D2/6.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is D2/6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I propose we will come back to this issue after the coffee break also to check the difference between D6/6 and D2/6. Let me now say to Mr. Vidovic, good morning, good morning, Mr. Vidovic. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Krajina:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please give us your name, the year of your birth, and your address?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Alojz Vidovic, father Niko, born on the 13th of February, 1937, Pirici-Santici, the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, since when have you been living at your current place of residence?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since 1964.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Vlatko Kupreskic and his family?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I've known Vlatko since he was a boy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, on the 16th of April, 1993, that is, on the day of the conflict in Ahmici, where were you then?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the morning, when did you get up?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Around half past 5.00, around half past 5.00, I was woken up by shots fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I got up, I got ready. I had a pig, so I give it something to eat, and then I went to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go? What shelter, where?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Jozo Vrebac's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is it from your house, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's about 100 metres by an asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could get there in no time?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, why did you go to that particular shelter? What kind of a shelter is it? Can you describe it a little?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that shelter is safe, and naturally I went there to get away from the shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to that shelter before?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, before, when the aircraft of the Yugo army would come and when there would be an alert, then we would go all to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, when is it that you arrived at the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been around a quarter to 6 -- approximately, because I never looked at the watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in the shelter until the next day, but naturally, since my house was close, I did go back there to get some candles and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us, that morning, when you got to the shelter, for how long were you there without going out?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was there until 12.00. I did not go out. That is, I did get out of the shelter, but I didn't go back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where were you?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, on the basis of what you have just told us, can we then say that you spent in that shelter between 6.00 in the morning until 12.00 on the 16th, all the time?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during that period of time when you were in the shelter, did you see Vlatko Kupreskic or some of the members of his family? Will you please tell us, whom did you see?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Vlatko when he arrived with his wife, two children, and his mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So at what time did they get there?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was around 6.00, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around 6.00. So could you tell us what did Vlatko look like, what was he wearing? Was it civilian clothes, or uniform, or whether he had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was in civilian clothes, and he did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long did Vlatko stay in the shelter after he entered it?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Vlatko was there until 10.00 or thereabouts and then he left. And his Uncle Anto asked him, "Where are you going," and he said, "I'm going to see my old man."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that or see that?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it and I heard it, because I was standing with his Uncle Anto in front of the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he said he was going to see his father?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know if Vlatko came back to the shelter again?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When could that have been?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was around half past 3.00 or 4.00. That is when he came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear him say something then?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Anto asked him again then how was it, and he said, "He's fine, he's all right, he's alive."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is that Anto?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That Anto is his father's brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was enquiring about Vlatko's father?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, that shelter, were there mostly elderly and women and children who were there or --

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but naturally there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you surprised to see Vlatko there because he was relatively young?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a surprise, because I knew he was not fit for the army, since he had been operated on when he was a child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do the military service?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not. I know that for certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else, please. Do you know if Vlatko Kupreskic, before April '93 or ever, was he politically active? Did he ever join any formations or anything?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Vlatko was never interested in politics. The only thing he's interested in is business. That's his, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you showed like this, that gesture that you made, what does it mean? It's a gesture indicating a man who is trying to make some money or what?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's his concern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was that the only thing that Vlatko did at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely the only thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Vidovic, please, I shall now move on and show you two documents. First I should like to ask the usher to distribute these documents to Their Honours, to the Prosecution and the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit will be marked D43/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, did you see this document?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it about?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is about my son, Mirko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vidovic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Vidovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His place of residence, his address, would you have a look at it? This is a certificate of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That he lived in Travnik, that is, the municipality, and I know that. I mean he was there throughout the war. He never came over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So this is a certificate saying that your son, Mirko Vidovic, lived and lives in Travnik. The address we have here, the name of the street?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: All right. Now I will show you yet another document. Will you please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, meanwhile, as this document is distributed, let me ask you, Mr. Vidovic, are there more people in that area where you live of that same name, Mirko Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My brother -- my cousin, my son, and there's a third relative who --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They are all Mirko?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are all Mirkos. Mirko Vidovic, that is my cousin Niko's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. He's your cousin. According to this certificate, where does he live?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He lives in Vitez. He has a flat there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have also the name of the street here, don't we? It's Kresimira, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Kresimira.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 4?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, number 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any other Mirko Vidovic? Jozo's son?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is my uncle's son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does he live?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He lives across from Vlatko's wholesale unit. He has a house there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he was in '93?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Germany. Did he spend some time there?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, thank you. I have only one more question for you and that will be it. I don't remember asking you, but let me repeat it. Do you remember if Vlatko's father ever came to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did he come to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He came around 8.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he come?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Vlatko was with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he looked like? Was he ill?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he looked sad and he was sick. He had this leg, problematic leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he came with a stick?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had a stick with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Vidovic. I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have finished.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The previous exhibit will be marked D44/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I should like to tender these two documents into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, I would have only one observation in relation to them, Your Honours, and that is this: That as certificates, they purport -- or I suggest, with respect, that they prove only the information contained in that certificate as being valid at the 29th of April, 1999, the date of the making. The actual duration of residence by either of these parties at those residences isn't shown on the documents. I say that just as a point of evidence. As to whatever weight you attach to that is a matter for you, but I thought I'd point it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So they are admitted into evidence. Any cross-examination by other Defence counsel? I don't see anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Vidovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: My name is Michael Blaxill. I'm one of the Prosecution counsel working in this case. I would like to ask you a few questions as a result of what you have told the Chamber this morning. Cross-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you say you were awakened by shooting that you heard at about half past 5.00 on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You got up and got dressed. Can you tell me what clothing you put on that day, what sort of clothing?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Civilian, the usual. I had a fur-lined jacket because it was cold at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the colour of the jacket, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was the olive-brown-gray colour, because it was from the company -- it was from the stock of the company, and I worked for the company, and I took it home. It has some fur inside, but it looked mostly olive-green-brown colour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then, having fed your pig, you went to the shelter, you said, of Jozo Vrebac; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is, yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that, in fact, the house that is occupied by the daughter of Mr. Vrebac?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall, what is the layout of the shelter that is created within that building?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can, yes. There is a passage, and from the passage one goes down to the shelter. Downstairs, there are three rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at that building, did you yourself go down into those basement rooms?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went down to the basement by myself, as my brother was already there. He had gone down there before me. But he had a stroke, and his sons carried him away. So I saw that he had been taken care of, and then I started down. But as many people were smoking there and I'm not a smoker, I came out. I simply couldn't stand that air down there. I don't smoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say that the conditions at that time were very crowded? Were there a lot of people there?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not at the beginning. But, yes, later on, rather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've been told this very morning, sir, that shortly after 5.00, a group of villagers of some 25 families or more had already turned up at the Vrebac household to go to the shelter. Would you say that when you went into the basement area, there were the equivalent of 25 families in there, let's say 70, 80 people?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. That family came the next day. It's from a small family. The next day, when somebody revealed that the Mujahedin had broken through the front line, then they came from Mahala, and the shelter was empty because they had gone to Rovna in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think possibly in the course of --

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then these people from Mahala came and took their place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we have a misunderstanding. Mr. Vidovic, what I would like to know, if I may, please, is when you went down into that basement, do you think there were perhaps 70 or 80 people actually in there sheltering?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. While I was there, no, there weren't that many at all. Only the people close by were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me a name or a few names of the few of the people you saw there?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: For instance, there was the Livancics, Vrebac, Vidovic, Kovac, Martinovic families, --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did --

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- several more, but that was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the number of people sheltering in that basement increase to a large number?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As time passed, more and more people came. Of course, most of them were children and elderly people and women. Some were even brought in wheelbarrows, those who couldn't walk on their own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing the arrival of any members of the Kupreskic family?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that all the Kupreskics came. Mica brought his mother-in-law in a wheelbarrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "all the Kupreskics", that included, did it not, Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic, his wife and children?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Only the father was missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only the father was missing?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. The father wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Kupreskic family, Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic and his wife and his children, arrived at the shelter, can you tell me where they went? Did they go down to the basement or to some other part of the building?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They went to the basement. Vlatko came back quickly and sat with us in the hallway. He came up from the basement. Probably he couldn't stand the close air down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you remained in the hallway. Do you recall the movements of Mr. Jozo Vrebac? Was he in the hall, was he in the basement, or was he in and out of the building?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Jozo Vrebac was also in the hallway and in the basement, and he was moving around all over the place because it is all his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he in fact leave the building at any times?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From that building?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that building.

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: His house is nearby, so it was normal for him to go to his house as well. His house is L-shaped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, while you were in that hallway, what was Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic wearing?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Civilian clothes, I know that. But I really can't remember what I was wearing, considering what it was like, and anyway, it's a long time ago. I've forgotten myself. I remember wearing that thick winter jacket, but that's all. But I know 100 per cent that he was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you couldn't, for instance, describe whether that was a jacket or a woollen thing or what colour it was or something like that that he wore on top, or the colour of his trousers?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was a jacket that he was wearing. I think it was a jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be true to say, sir, that at that time the assembled people were very frightened and they were agitated at what was going on; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. All of us were distressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, as people, taking a look outside the building to see what you could see that was happening in the village of Ahmici and around?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All we could see from there was smoke. We couldn't tell whose houses were affected. We could just see the smoke and hear the shooting, because our view was obstructed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this unique and very distressing situation, sir, would it be true to say that you did not really keep track of time with any great accuracy; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't even have a watch. All I'm saying is very roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So sometime later, you say that Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic said he was going to see, quote, I think you said, "To go see my old man," and he left the shelter area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So taking account of what you have just said about the conditions and what you've just said about the passage of time, what you've said about not having a watch or paying attention to that, can you honestly say, sir, that you're so sure he left the shelter at 10.00?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I said "10.00," I said "approximately 10.00."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even an approximation to that hour, I would suggest, sir, is something you could not today rely on with certainty, can you? You weren't paying attention to the time when these terrible events were taking place; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying again that what I said was "approximately." I didn't claim otherwise. I said "approximately." It could have been a little earlier, a little later, but somewhere about then. It doesn't mean exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I thank you for answering my questions, Mr. Vidovic. Thank you, Your Honours. That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a question, Mr. Vidovic. Mr. Vidovic, when did you realise, on the 16th or 17th of April, that a lot of killing had taken place in Ahmici and that quite a few houses were on fire?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, we learned about it. We were very confused, and on the 17th, when we learned about it all, we were even more distressed because it affected all of us. It surprised us. We had never expected any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any Croatian house on fire or destroyed by shelling?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't see from where we were, we couldn't see anything. But the next day, when the mist had lifted, one could see only the ruins. But those of us who were there, we didn't know. There was people coming to tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is as follows, Mr. Vidovic: After such a terrible event, I mean anybody would, I assume, ask himself or herself, "Who did all this killing and burning?" Did you ask yourself this question? Did you ask your neighbours? Did you discuss this matter with your friends and neighbours?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I knew, I would name him immediately, if he were my own son, and I know for sure that it wasn't these men who are sitting here. I can guarantee that, --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but still I --

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- because a crime was indeed committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But as I say, did you make any guess about the possible authors of those crimes? Did your neighbours tell you anything, or your friends or your acquaintances?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All I know is that none of our neighbours could have done it or did it. And also when the crime was committed against Croats, I'm sure that the neighbours could not have been the perpetrators. Of that I am sure, personally, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vidovic. I assume there's no objection to the witness being released. Thank you so much for giving evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're very welcome. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, our next witness, Ruza Grgic, has been ordered to come to the courtroom at 10.30, because that is how we assumed that the time would be used up. So as we have finished ahead of time, perhaps she hasn't been brought yet, so perhaps we could have our break now and resume work at 10.30 or a few minutes after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. It's a very good suggestion, but I think we now deserve a 30-minute break, because today we will take only one break. So we will resume at, say, 20 to 11.00. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, madam. Could you please stand and make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Krajina:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us first your name, when you were born, and what is your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I am Ruza Grgic, born on the 9th of May, 1949, in Putis. I live in the village of Pirici, municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell us, what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I'm a housewife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us, since when have you been living in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I have been living in Pirici since 1979.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the time?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: All the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us if you know Vlatko Kupreskic and his family?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I know him very well indeed, and I knew them in those years, both Vlatko and his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember, on the 16th of April, 1993, that is, on the day of the conflict in Ahmici, could you perhaps tell us, where were you on that day, and what did you do then? Also, can you tell us if you saw Vlatko Kupreskic that particular day?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: That morning, around 5.00 or half past 5.00, Niko Sakic came to wake us up and to tell us to go to the shelter immediately. So I picked up my children in a rush; we collected only the basic necessities. In about five or six minutes we were at the shelter, and there we already found children and women and old people. We stayed there. We went down to the lower basement. We also went upstairs, and that is where I saw Vlatko Kupreskic and his mother and his wife and his two children. We stayed there that day, that night, and the next day until the evening. That day, around 10.00, an opportunity presented itself. It was around breakfast time. I remember we felt peckish, and I heard Vlatko say, "I should go and see if my father is still alive; I should go home." So then Vlatko went home, and around 4.00, 3.00 or 4.00, I again saw Vlatko come back and say that his father was well and alive. So we were still together, again looked for shelter, then would come out, then would go back down to the lower part of the basement because the toilet was upstairs. So sometime in late afternoon, when Vlatko's father came, and he was sitting upstairs next to the door, because he was a sick man; he could barely walk. He had a stick, and he was smoking. It was difficult for him to come down to the basement, so he was sitting on a bench next to the door, and I remember well Vlatko's dad. And so that was that. And that night we were there all together. In the morning, again, it was the same thing, until the evening. And in the evening, we saw that it became dangerous there, and we said, "We're going to Rovna because it's not safe for us any more here." We set off to Rovna all together. So we went and reached Rovna, and there we dispersed, depending on who would take us in. I went to Slavko Santic's house with my family, and we stayed the night there, and others stayed in other houses. We stayed the night there, and in the morning, we again peered out to see where was who, and how people had been put up, and I saw Vlatko again, how he had brought some food for his wife and children, and we saw him, as he had some toiletries under his arm, and that was something that we needed, and that is how I remembered him. Well, and then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah, all right, but how long did you stay in Rovna?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Rovna until noon or thereabouts, and then I went to Vitez. I had my uncle there, my husband's brother, and we spoke by telephone, and I heard that one of my sons had fallen ill, and he went to see a doctor in Vitez. He was running a very high fever. So I moved from Rovna with the other children to Vitez, and there I found my son. He was ill; he was given an infusion. Then two or three days later my husband came, and he told me to go home and that the children would stay there. He said, "I haven't had any warm food for so many days," so that I should go back with him to our house to cook something for him. So we left our children with my husband's brother, and my husband and I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back a little, please, to that day when you were still in the shelter. Let me just ask you briefly: Do you remember Vlatko, when he came to the shelter, what was he wearing, civilian or military clothes?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Vlatko was in civilian, absolutely. I do remember his jacket, which was the colour of chocolates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any weapons or something?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: No, he did not have any weapons. He never had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I think that will suffice. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination by the Defence counsel? No? Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Franck Terrier, and I shall ask you several questions on behalf of the Prosecution with regard to your testimony. Could you please tell us, where is your house in Santici?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: My house is above Niko Sakic's house, above the road of Niko Sakic, in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific: How far is your house from Niko Sakic's house?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Well, about a minute's walk. Not more than two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us about your family. Could you tell us, who were members of your household at that time? I'm talking about April '93. Who were the members of your household at the time? Who was living with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I was living with my husband and my two sons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give me the name, the first name of your husband, please?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Drago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give me the names and the age of your two sons?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: My older son is called Mirko; he was born in 1969. The other son was called Mladen, and he was born in 1982.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your house, at the time when it happened, were you and your two sons in the house?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were all together in the house until that morning. That morning, with the younger son, I went to the shelter. My elder son was not feeling well, so he stayed at home, and my husband also stayed home. We had some cows, and we also had some lambs, and they had to be fed. So my husband said, "You two go, and we shall come later." This older son was rather unwell at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time of the day did you see again your husband and your elder son?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I did not see my elder son again until I went from Rovna to Vitez. That day, when we were in the shelter, my son was taken away to see a doctor in Vitez, since he had fallen ill. He had a very high fever. When I was in Rovna, then I spoke with my brother-in-law by telephone, and he told me that I should go to Vitez straight away because my elder son had arrived and was staying with him, and he had been to see the doctor, and he was then back in my husband's brother's house, bedridden there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shall we be more precise? When did your son who had fallen ill been to a doctor in Vitez? Which day was that?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: The first time, the 16th of April, that morning when we went to the shelter, they stayed at home, and that same day he fell ill and went to Vitez, and I knew nothing about him. I had no news of him until the evening of the next day that we were spending at Rovna. And then the next morning, I spoke to my brother-in-law in Vitez, and that is what my brother-in-law told me. He told me that the son had arrived that morning on the 16th; that when we went to the shelter, that my son had gone to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was the 16th of April, 1993, when your eldest son, who was not feeling well, stayed at home and then went to see a doctor in Vitez; is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is so. It is true, yes, because -- well, I'm not quite sure about who did he go with. How did he go there, I don't know that. I don't really remember that because it was so difficult to find out, to find out the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any weapons at your place?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: No, there were never any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not even some hunting weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: No. There were no weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any member of your family a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: No, there were never. They never went to any army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember at what time, approximately, and you may not remember, but at about what time did you leave your home with your youngest son to go to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: It was around 5.00 or half past 5.00, and it took us about five or six minutes to get to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the shelter, did the fire already start?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: When we got to the shelter, yes, there was already shooting, and we sought shelter in the lower part. Then when it abated slightly, we would come out and look around, take a peek around, but very little we did that. We spent it mostly downstairs. But we had to go upstairs because the bathroom was upstairs, so we would come out once in a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back a little. Who was it that told you to go to the shelter of Rebac's house rather than to some other place?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: It was Niko Sakic who told us to go to Jozo Vrebac's shelter, as it was the safest, it was well dug into the ground and it was the best place, and we really found that it was the place where we would feel best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Niko Sakic have any particular duty?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: No, never. He was a man of rather advanced age. I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been to this shelter of Jozo Vrebac before the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: No, we were never. I was there before. When there were planes, I was in Niko Sakic's shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you arrived in Vrebac's shelter, you went down to the basement; is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were in the basement, and then we came upstairs and we would spend some time upstairs. As soon as the fire would abate, we would come up. Then when there would be more intensive fire, we would go downstairs. And then when it would calm down again, we would come upstairs to get some milk because children were not feeling well. It was very close air there, and there were some people who were ill there. For a while, we had some electricity, but then the power was cut off, so candles had to be lit. And so we were spending time there but then we wouldn't have enough air to breathe, and they would come up and then go down again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, how many people were there in the basement?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Oh, dear, who could tell that? I mean there were so many of us, nobody counted them. But there were very many people because it was really -- I mean it was really the safest place. But there were very many of us, and there were ill people and elderly and women and children. I also remember that same Vlatko's son was sick, and he took him to the bathroom but he threw up in the passage in the hallway, and I really felt very sorry for that child. Somebody brought a towel to clean it up. I felt very sorry, and Vlatko had him in his lap as the child threw up. Of course, it was so hard. I mean children, our children, after all. It was very difficult. We were very distressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you a photograph, with the help of the usher. It is D13/3. I should like to ask you to look at all these photographs and to confirm if that is the case, that this is the house where you found shelter, and to tell us whether you see the room in which you took shelter.

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: No, it can't be seen here. That is the house, that is the house (indicating). This is where I saw Vlatko for the first time, on these steps (indicating). He was smoking. Then we went in.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness use the other microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: This is where the toilet is (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To facilitate understanding, could you indicate the number of the photograph you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: This is the first photograph showing Jozo Vrebac's daughter's -- or rather son-in-law's house, and that is where we entered. Then there are steps leading to the basement. We stayed there. In the hallway, the toilet is here (indicating). We would come out to the steps sometimes. Then we would go back inside to the basement. We would spend some time in the rooms, when the shooting was not so intense, and we would see each other. We spent a lot of time there together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, could you tell us, on these photographs, the place where you saw Vlatko Kupreskic for the first time that morning?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Here (indicating) on these steps, I saw Vlatko Kupreskic smoking that morning. His wife and children were in there (indicating). When I came out, I saw them. Vlatko's father was in there. There was a bench. He was next to the door, closer to the door, so he would have more air. He smoked there, here in front of the door (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is where you saw him for the first time. Who was the first to reach the shelter? Was it you or his family?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: One couldn't tell when people arrived. Just the short period that we walked up and down, I remember seeing Vlatko in the morning. It can't have been long after I arrived, because when I went to the toilet, I saw Vlatko, his wife, the two children. His father had still been at home. Then he left again around 10.00, Vlatko did, and he saw that his father was alive. In the afternoon, they brought him over, and all of us stayed there in this shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that things are quite clear, when you saw Vlatko Kupreskic for the first time that morning, you were already in the shelter for some time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I came in and out. We weren't in one place. We would move around. We were all nervous. It was hard for us. It wasn't just the simple case of going downstairs and sitting there. You had to walk around. This was the first time in our life. We never were exposed to such danger before, until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand very well, madam. Could you still tell us more clearly, for how long had you been in the shelter when you saw Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Well, who could tell? It wasn't long. It was soon after that. We looked around to see who was there, who had arrived, who had stayed on at home. That was how it was. And all of us who were close, we would rally there, and that is where we got together. There were a lot of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a watch, madam?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: A watch? Yes, I do have a watch. You mean did I have a watch then?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is my question, at the time.

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a watch, but I knew roughly the morning, when it was morning, then noon, afternoon. We could tell by the light. I didn't look at my watch. I didn't have one, anyway. I may have asked somebody what time it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you had a very approximate notion of the time; morning, midday, afternoon. These are rough estimates; you would agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly.
