I think it was about 10.00, because the children were already hungry, they wanted to have something to eat, and somebody would give something to one child, somebody to another. Whatever we had, we shared. So this was about breakfast time. Then I heard Vlatko saying that he wanted to go and see whether his father was alive, and Vlatko left. We stayed on in the same way, and then I saw Vlatko again in the afternoon, perhaps it was 3.00 or 4.00, and he said that his father was alive. Then he brought his father towards the evening. We spent the night there. We were all together. No one went anywhere then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Allow me to interrupt you to go back to this question of time. If I understood you well, you said that Vlatko Kupreskic left the shelter around 10.00 on the basis of the fact that it was the time for breakfast, and you said it was time for breakfast because the children were hungry?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I think it was. I hope it was about 10.00 when we had sort of calmed down, the shooting had subsided a little, and then we thought we would give the children something to eat, and that is how I saw Vlatko then. It was about 10.00, not more. But I saw him before that, too, in the morning. But it was then that he went to see his father, about 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you always have Vlatko Kupreskic in sight or would it be possible for him to be absent for a time before this moment that you said was 10.00 when he left?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: He didn't go anywhere. Vlatko was there with us, his wife and children. Where would he go and leave his wife and children and mother behind? Where could he go? We were all there together, protecting each other. The only thing was that he thought about his father, who he had left at home, and so about 10.00 he went back to see whether his father was alive. Then he said that his father was alive and well, and he came back about 3.00 or 4.00. I think that is when I saw him, about that time. Then he went back again to fetch his father, and they came, and we stayed there together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Allow me to ask you whether it is customary to have breakfast at 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, it depends on the habits. It wasn't customary. It depended how every household was run. Some people eat earlier on, some later. But as everything was upset, so nobody ate regularly. People ate when they could and when it was quieter. When the children became hungry, they asked for something to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I think that you said a moment ago that there were some sick people in this shelter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were people who were ill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, but not your son -- why didn't they go to see a doctor, like your son did?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: My son was younger. These people were elderly, and they had been ill for some time. A woman called Jela, her daughter was with her. She kept giving her medicine, and they brought her in a wheelbarrow to the shelter. So we didn't know what to do with her afterwards. She was very ill. Jela Vidovic was her name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't you surprised not to see Vlatko Kupreskic's father?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: The father wasn't there in the morning straightaway. He came towards nightfall on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that Vlatko Kupreskic's father was not there in the shelter in the morning, but my question is the following: My question was weren't you surprised not to see Vlatko Kupreskic's father?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Well, we knew that he was ill, and why he didn't come immediately, perhaps he still felt safe staying on in his house. Who knows? So he stayed behind. He didn't come that morning. He only came towards evening. But Jela was brought over because she was totally bedridden. And there was some others who were elderly and sick, and we were all there under those very difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is that it is possible, from your point of view, that Vlatko Kupreskic's father felt he was safer staying at home than coming to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you -- I can't know now. How do I know what the man thought? I can't remember that. I just remember when I saw him. As to what his decision was, I don't know. We fled, each as best they could. Nobody looked at others, where people were running or going. We ran away to the closest safe place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did your husband do during that day?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: On that day I stayed at home; I didn't see him until he came to fetch me in Vitez to take me home. We hadn't heard or seen each other. He said, "You go with the others," that I should flee to protect the children, and he stayed on to take care of the cows, the lambs. He said he would stay at home. So I didn't see him again until we reached Vitez, his brother's place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband tell you what he had done in the course of that day?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I never asked him. The important thing was that we saw each other, that we were alive and well. That is all we cared about. And then he said that I should go home with him and leave the children there because it was safer in Vitez than in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he never said anything about what he had done in the course of that day, and you never asked him the question?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: No, I never asked him anything. I just got ready and went home with him, and the children stayed behind. Those were hard times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean that you left Vitez to return to Santici, leaving the children in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date did you return home?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: Well, after spending the night in Rovna, the next day, in the evening, I went to Vitez. I spent only one night in Vitez. I saw my son then, and we stayed there about two days. Two days later my husband came. He came on foot, via Rijeka, and he said that we should also go through Rijeka because it was safer, and we returned home to give him a cooked meal. He said he hadn't eaten anything, just some dry rations. And that is how the children stayed on for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you returned home on the Tuesday or Wednesday following the 16th of April, which was a Friday?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: We fled on the Friday, the 16th, then came Saturday, Sunday evening, and then we spent the night -- one night in Rovna, and the next evening we went to Vitez, where we stayed one or two days; I'm not sure about that. I know that my husband came shortly after that to see how my son was, because he was still very ill, and he said that I should go home. What day it was I really cannot recollect exactly, because one gets confused about the days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You confuse days and times, yet you know what time Vlatko Kupreskic left the shelter at Jozo Vrebac's place?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I got there about 5.00, 5.30, and maybe 15 minutes or half an hour later, on the outside, I didn't see him. We left our bags, we looked around the basement, and we immediately came back upstairs, and that is when I saw him on the steps, smoking. His wife was there and his children were there and his mother, and that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, when you went back to your home at the request of your husband, in the week that followed the 16th of April, what was the situation like in the village? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anything. We would work a little, we would do planting in the garden, when there was no shooting. When the shooting started, we would seek shelter. We looked after the lambs, we fed the cow. At night time, again, the few of us that were in a village would get together in one house and spend the night, to be together, and that is how we lived through those times. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the people who were in the village in this period that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: I do remember. I remember Gavro; he was my neighbour. Brnada. We went to spend the night at his place. Gavro had his uncle, so we would stay there. It was safer there, so we spent the night there, at his place, for a couple of nights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when you saw Vlatko Kupreskic again, and his family?

utterances.speaker: RUZA GRGIC
utterances.text: My husband, later, we just stayed at home. We couldn't see each other much; only the people close by we saw from time to time. People hid and sought protection, so I don't know anything more about Vlatko and his family -- at the time, while the shooting went on, and while the war continued. Afterwards, we saw each other again, we would see each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We don't have any questions. So I assume the witness may be released. Madam, thank you. You may be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness, on behalf of the Court, I can tell Counsel Susak that, indeed, we will resume on the 21st of June, and we will be sitting the whole of that week. However, the following week, we can't sit in Kupreskic because we have another case and then the plenary meeting, so there will be a gap. So we will, as I say, sit in this case only in the week starting on the 21st of June, for one week. We will resume, then, in July, the week starting on the Monday, 5th of July, until the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to hear from Your Honours whether the witnesses of Drago Josipovic will be able to testify in this period from the 21st to the 25th of June this year. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Vidovic. Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Krajina:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Court your name, the date of your birth, your place of residence, and what you do.

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Fikreta Vidovic, born on the 23rd of April, 1944, in Vitez, Bosnia and Herzegovina. My parents are Muslims. I have no specific ethnicity. I'm an educator. I am at present in Santici elementary school in Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, do you know Vlatko Kupreskic and his family?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you known them?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I've known him since his first grade in school. I was his teacher from the first to the fourth grade. And after that, of course, I watched him grow up. I was also his brother's -- or rather his sister's teacher; he doesn't have a brother. And I've always -- and the relations between his family and myself -- well, you know, I'm a teacher, and they were his parents, and we were quite close because I was really keeping an eye on how he grew up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was rather a different pupil, because he had had heart surgery in his second grade, so he was two months behind, in other words, so that I would take his homework back home, or whatever we had done at school, I would take it to his home so that he could keep pace with us. After that, at the recommendation of physicians, he didn't have to do any physical culture, any exercises. So I had to keep him apart, and I would do some light exercises, physical exercises, with him, or simply separate him from other children because of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Could you please tell us -- I presume you do have an opinion of that boy. What do you think about him as a man, the character, the kind of man, his behaviour before the war, and even during the war and after that. Could you please tell us something about him?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since I did really follow how he grew up, and it wasn't all that easy with us to go to the university and complete one's studies, when you come from a modest family, as his was. So we did, yes, keep in touch. We would meet in the street, or I went to visit his parents, or when they would come to visit me, then I would always ask them, "Well, how is Vlatko? Is he all right?" And I was happy to hear that he got married, and then when he had his first child, that is, a girl, Milena, and things like that. After that, I was his son's teacher, so I can say only the best about Vlatko. He was a child that every parent would want to have, a friend that anybody would like to have as a friend, a person who would never hurt a fly. He is really the best of sons, the best of friends, and he always worked hand in hand with his neighbours, was co-operative with -- always lent a hand to his neighbours. He had very broad circles of friends. I don't think anybody could hold anything against him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you also give us your impression, or your opinion, as to Vlatko's attitude to other people in his milieu, in his environment, especially people of different ethnic origin; and also, if you know anything about that, what was his attitude towards Muslims, his neighbours and others?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do have my opinion about that. I used to say he was a humanist. He was man who never paid any attention to what particular ethnic group somebody came from. He only wanted to know if somebody was a good or a bad man, just as we all did. So he always lent a hand and worked together with his neighbours, Muslims, and I don't think any one of them could have any bad opinion about him or say anything bad about his work or about what he did or how he did it, because whatever he did, he always helped and was cooperative as a man and neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're an educator, you're a teacher. In that particular environment, you must have had a rather broad circle of acquaintances, and you must be often in touch with people from the area. So could you tell us if you have heard anyone, ever, say anything bad about Vlatko Kupreskic, about how he behaved before the war, during, or after the war?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I have never heard anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us you are a teacher at the elementary school in Ahmici, so could you tell us, prior to the 16th of April, '93, until when could you have regular instruction?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember very well that day because that was when my daughter returned. We had classes between 13.00 and 15.45. We had to cut down, of course, on the schedule, because of the shelling, so we cut down the classes, and the instruction -- we did sustain the instruction somehow, but we had to have shorter classes so the children could get back before -- get home before dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are referring to the period before that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm saying about the 15th of April, we had regular classes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So regular classes on the 15th of April, you said, between 13.00 till 15.45?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have both children of Croat and Muslim ethnicity present?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all those children attended classes on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was regular instruction?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. We also asked parents, called parents; we were asking them to work with the children, pay more attention, because the end of the term was coming near, so that on that particular day we had a meeting with parents to tell them to pay more attention to these children in view of all the circumstances, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- right. Did everything look normal to you these days, I mean, at school, in your conversations with parents, and all that, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A while ago you mentioned that your daughter had come from a foreign country. Could you tell us, what country did your daughter come from, and when was it that she came back to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the shelling of Vitez started, my daughter left -- or rather two days before the Vitezit was shelled, she went to Paris, to my brother, because she was afraid. She had small children, and she was a single mother, and we wanted to protect her because she was afraid. It was major psychological stress. She had gone to Paris, and she was in Paris -- that was Monday when she arrived in Split, so it could have been the 13th -- or perhaps the 14th; I can't really remember the date. But in any event, she arrived in Split on Monday. My husband went to fetch her by car, and on Rostovo there was some block, and then he returned the next day home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you properly, your daughter returned from Paris to Ahmici on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but when we talked, she said, "You know, it's safe enough, and I can't live without you; I want to come back home." And that was that. That was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you thought it was safe enough for her to come back home?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, we thought it was quite all right. Otherwise we would have talked her out of coming back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Vlatko had had a heart operation when he was a small boy?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any further consequences of that surgery? What was his health after that? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know when that time before the military service came, I know he was relieved of the military service with the Yugoslav People's Army because of his heart condition, because he was a special case, because he had had this heart operation, and it was one of those serious health problems for which you could be relieved of the military service, from serving their term with the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And only two brief questions more; we shall be over in our time, Mrs. Vidovic. Could you tell us something about something that I guess you have some knowledge about, since you were -- you came from the area, and you did follow what happened to your former pupil: Do you know if, at any time whatsoever, Vlatko was active in politics, was engaged in politics, was he a member of any political party organisation, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you, because I did talk to him about these things, and the situation was like that. No, he was absolutely indifferent to it. He simply didn't want to talk about that. There were more of us like that -- I mean, people who were not interested in politics at all, and Vlatko is one of those people who are completely indifferent to politics. He simply looked -- you know, about bread, as we put it in our country; that is, business, economy, things like that. He was completely indifferent to politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question more: Have you ever seen Vlatko wearing a uniform or carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Vidovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I have completed my examination of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Krajina. Yes, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Susak also would like to ask some questions. Sorry, I didn't know. So it is Mr. Susak and then Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Susak:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you a few questions only, Mrs. Vidovic. Would you please tell us, where is your house, precisely?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My house is in Santici, about 20 metres away from the main Travnik/Lasva road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or in other words, the Vitez/Kaonik road?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are by the road, and across the road, whose houses are they? Do you know which were Ramiz, Nazif Ahmic houses, and others?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is their position in relation to your house?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that one is to the south-east and the other one south-west, if I may say so. Across from my house is a meadow. That is, if I look from my house, in relation to -- below my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll help you. You said that your house was by the road, and across the road are some houses belonging to --

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ramiz, Nazif, and the third Ahmic house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far from the road are they, from your house?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I should say as far from the road as mine is. That was the plan. You couldn't build it right next by the road; there had to be a distance of at least 20 metres from the road. That is where you could build.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, I was in your yard and I was over there. Could you tell us how far are these houses away from the road? How far from the road are these houses, because they are farther away from the road than your house?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they could have been less than 20 metres, they could have been more than 20 metres away, so that it could be 30 metres or so. I've never measured it. I never had any need to. But a bit farther away from the road than my houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it more or less than 50 metres?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, thereabouts. Could be about 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the road, in relation to Ramiz and Nazif Ahmics' and other Ahmics' house, is there a hedge?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the hedge?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's green. They planted it as protection from dust. We call it shrubbery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How tall is it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's up to a metre, because they trimmed it. Now, of course, it's much, much taller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the houses of Musafer Puscul and Hasim Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far are these houses from the road, roughly?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: About 30 metres, but they are, well -- no, I never had an eye for these distances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean they are closer, that the houses of Hasim Ahmic and Musafer Puscul are, in fact, also houses very close to the road?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That Ogrjev or, rather, the storage space of Ogrjev is near your house?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a kind of village road between Hasim Ahmic's house and Ogrjev storage space?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this path lead?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It led to a shop, and we also used it as a shortcut to the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Across that path, across that village road, is there a fence, or does that railing fencing engulf the storage space of Ogrjev?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know there is a fence, but I didn't really pay any attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I see. Right, thank you. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, Mrs. Vidovic. I also have a few questions only. Cross-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know their families?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do; father, mother, sister, the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you friends with their parents and their families throughout this time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Ever since I began working there to this day, we've always been friends, I suppose we would call it, very good friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Could you tell us, what kind of a family was it, since you were on close terms with them? What kind of parents were they? And Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, how were they brought up?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is a nice, modest family, and their goal in life was to bring up their children, to provide them with as much education as they could afford. And I think they even went beyond that, because this is a rather humble family and only the father worked, and there were three children who practically went to school at one and the same time, and they needed a lot of money to provide it for them. It was a family which devoted all their life of putting their children straight, bringing them up and giving them as much schooling as they could. As I said, they came from very humble origins, but then they were provided with secondary education, and then they found jobs and continued their studies and started standing on their own feet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there in Ahmici, as you were in touch with them, their families and themselves, were there ever any problems? Were they problem children?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. The children spent all their leisure time playing music. I don't think that people who play music, like musical select people, it is simply beyond me how somebody who opts for such a way of life can hold any grudge against somebody else for whatever reason. That is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. Yes, Counsel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I also indicated I would have a question, also a comment to make. Good morning, I'm Petar Pavkovic. I'm a lawyer. Cross-examined by Mr. Pavkovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your daughter came back from Paris on the eve of these events. She left because she was afraid, and she returned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said, "Yes, she thought it was safe."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were a teacher, which means that you necessarily communicate with very many people?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you agree with me that you were a person who was well informed or, rather, better informed than many other people in that place where you communicated with many people?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends. It depends on what -- on the subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean generally.

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm a person who never meddled in politics and I was completely indifferent to politics. My concern were children, so it was the children, it was cooperating with their parents, rather that humane side of it. And it was -- by and large, it was that particular field, of course, of life that I was very familiar with where I lived and where I still live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were with your daughter immediately after she -- before she left, and you also kept in touch with her. You told her that the situation was such that she -- it was safe for her to come back? That was how you saw it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 14th of April, you had regular classes?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mrs. Vidovic, good afternoon to you. My name is Michael Blaxill, and I am one of the prosecuting counsel working on this case. I have just a very few questions I would like to ask you, madam, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you please slow down for the interpreters, Mr. Blaxill? Cross-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, you introduced yourself as an elementary school teacher in Dubravica. Is that where you actually practised your profession, or is that your residence, or both? I just want to be clear in my own mind.

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dubravica is the central school and Ahmici had a subsidiary school, and I live in Santici, which is a locality between Ahmici and Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said there was the sub-school in Ahmici. Were there any other schools in that immediate vicinity, in Pirici or Santici, or was that the only school?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was the only school in that part, in Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the date the 15th of April, 1993, had any other bodies of people or groups used the premises of the school in Ahmici? Was it used by anybody else other than just the school?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a humanitarian -- a room in school was used for the humanitarian food distribution. It was a classroom. It was our classroom. I believe the principal gave the authorisation, because somebody had to do it if we were to be left without a classroom. I do not know which humanitarian organisation was it, but I know it was a humanitarian body which then distributed flour and other food items amongst the villagers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, madam, do you know whether any form of military people used the school premises up to and including the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as -- no. As far as I know, no. You know, my working hours were between 13.00 to 15.45, and then I would go home. Outside those hours, I had nothing to do with the school, because my house is a little bit further away from the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you held normal class on the 15th of April, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the full number of children, both Croat children and Muslim children, at the classes that day?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, madam, were you able to -- when did the school reopen to teach children after the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the school in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't open, because it had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall -- just educate me in this, if you would, ma'am. Do you agree that the school premises were close to the premises of the -- I think it's the lower mosque in Ahmici. Were they near each other?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite close. Yes, quite near, or relatively. You know, two metres, five metres. I really don't have an eye for that. But, yes, they were nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I appreciate you worked very short hours in Ahmici for your teaching, but do you recall seeing the presence of any military-type people in or around the mosque on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one final point, if I may. You've described your contacts with the Kupreskic family over the years and enquiring after the health and prosperity and how Vlatko Kupreskic was doing. Did you have, in fact, much personal contact with Vlatko himself? Did you socialise together at all, or was your interest that of just a former teacher who kept in touch with the family and that's the kind of contact you had?

utterances.speaker: FIKRETA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is a practice I pursue. I keep in touch with my pupils as long as they are there on the spot, so that I really try to see how they are moving on. Then I teach their children. So we do keep -- so that we continue on good terms. And with Vlatko, yes, I did keep in touch, and I did communicate with him whenever he was around, because he plays music and all that and we talked about these things, and I liked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I have to ask. Thank you, ma'am, and thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I don't have any additional questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We don't have any questions either. I think there's no objection to the witness being released. Madam, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We can probably move on to our next witness. Yes, Counsel Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do not have any more witnesses here. We have one more witness, but we planned him for tomorrow, and he is to answer questions as to count 2. We really did not expect that it would be all so expedient and quick today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, I take this opportunity to commend both Counsel Krajina and Counsel Par, on behalf of the Court, for being so concise and to the point, and thanks to your being so, so that the pace of our proceedings has changed. So that means for today, we don't have any witness, so we will then adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00. Tomorrow, only one witness? Counsel Krajina, you have only one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and thank you very much for the kind words you addressed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We were wondering about the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for interrupting you. The rhythm -- the pace has changed, evidently, and I need to see when my witnesses will be coming. Now my accused urges me to ask if this schedule, as we agreed for the week of June 21st to 26th, does it still hold or not? The accused would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If I also may add something, evidently it depends also on our defence and the sequence of witnesses, I should like to tell you what we are planning to do. We have envisaged two groups of witnesses. With the first group, we shall finish tomorrow, and we have yet another set of witnesses. Next week, we are expecting seven witnesses. Four of them are expert witnesses. We are envisaging to complete our defence next week, and the rest -- I think by the 4th of June, I believe, we will have finished. We have witnesses as to count 2. These are expert witnesses. On that occasion, we shall also be showing several videotapes. To our mind, according to our reckoning, and of course it is based only on our plan, we do not know how much time the Prosecution will take, but we think that we shall fill in that whole week until the 4th of June. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Counsel Par. I think this is a good plan. So tomorrow we will hear one witness only, Mr. Vidovic, Stipan Vidovic, and then, if I understood you correctly, seven witnesses next week, and then you will have finished your case. Then on the 21st of June, we will start with the witnesses to be called by Counsel Susak. Is that fine with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You've helped me a great deal with this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. So we'll adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.00.
